# How LLMs work, for engineers {#sec-m02}

You do not need to build models to use them well. But a few facts about how they work explain most of what you will see in practice. This module shows them, mostly in pictures, and points you to free tools where you can try them yourself.

## Tokens: what the model actually reads

A model does not read words the way we do. It reads small pieces of text called **tokens**. @fig-tokens-words shows how a real tokenizer, the one used by OpenAI's GPT-4o models, splits a few words.

![Real splits from the GPT-4o tokenizer. Common words are one token; longer or rarer words are cut into pieces.](/figures/m02/tokens-words.pdf){#fig-tokens-words}

"Refund" is common, so it is one token. "Refunded" is two. "Unbelievable" is three. A made-up name like "Tarkika" is cut into "T", "ark" and "ika", because the model has never seen it as a whole. In English, 100 tokens is roughly 75 words.

Why should you care? Because everything about a model is counted in tokens. The price is per token. The speed is per token. The limit on how much you can send is in tokens.

Do not confuse a token with a **chunk**. A token is a tiny piece the model reads. A chunk is a large piece of a document, often a few hundred tokens, that you cut out yourself for searching. Chunks come in Module 7.

*Try it:* search for "OpenAI tokenizer" or open tiktokenizer.vercel.app. Paste any sentence and watch it split into coloured pieces, exactly like the figures here.

## The same message in five languages

Now look at @fig-tokens-playground. It is one message, "My refund has not come yet", written five ways, and split by the same tokenizer. A dot marks a space.

![One message, five ways, split by the GPT-4o tokenizer. Each coloured box is one token. The dotted circles in Hindi, Telugu and Kannada are pieces of a letter that the tokenizer cut away from the rest.](/figures/m02/tokens-playground.pdf){#fig-tokens-playground}

English needs 6 tokens. For the same meaning, Telugu needs 13, Hindi 14 and Kannada 16. In these scripts, the tokenizer often cuts a single letter into two pieces, like the vowel signs standing alone in their own boxes.

Why? The tokenizer learned its list of pieces mostly from English text. Common English words got their own tokens. Words in Indian scripts were seen less often, so they are built from many small pieces.

@fig-tokens-languages shows that this is improving, but not gone. The older GPT-4 tokenizer needed 29 tokens for the Hindi message, 36 for Telugu and 46 for Kannada. Studies across many languages find gaps of three to five times for Hindi, and up to fifteen times between some languages [@tokenpremium2026; @petrov2023].

![Tokens for the same message, counted with the older GPT-4 tokenizer and the newer GPT-4o tokenizer.](/figures/m02/tokens-languages.pdf){#fig-tokens-languages}

For your work, more tokens for the same message means a higher bill, a slower reply, and less room for anything else in the request. Hinglish, written in English letters, sits in between. If your users write in Indian languages, count a sample of their real messages before you plan a budget.

## Watching the model write

A model writes one token at a time. At each step it looks at all the text so far, gives every possible next token a chance, picks one, and adds it. Then it repeats. @fig-writing-steps shows four steps.

![The model writing a reply, one token per step. At each step it picks one token from many possible ones. (Chances made up for illustration.)](/figures/m02/writing-steps.pdf){#fig-writing-steps}

At step 1, "7" had an 85% chance, so it was picked. But "3" had 11%. Run the same request again, and sometimes the reply will say 3 days, not 7. Nothing is broken. The model is picking by chance, and the chances can go either way.

A setting called **temperature** controls how strongly the model prefers its top choice (@fig-next-token). At a low temperature, the top token wins almost every time. At a high temperature, the chances spread out and replies vary more.

![The same chances at two temperatures. Low temperature makes the top choice dominate; high temperature spreads the chances out. (Numbers made up for illustration.)](/figures/m02/next-token.pdf){#fig-next-token}

So your code must never expect one exact reply.

## How a model learns

Training is one simple exercise, repeated an enormous number of times (@fig-learning-loop). Hide the next word of a sentence. Let the model guess it. Check the guess. Then adjust the model a little, so that the right word becomes slightly more likely next time.

![Training in four steps. On the right: the chance the model gives the right word grows slowly as the loop repeats. (Numbers made up for illustration.)](/figures/m02/learning-loop.pdf){#fig-learning-loop}

One round changes almost nothing. Trillions of rounds, over text from the whole web, change everything. To get good at guessing the next word, the model has to learn grammar, facts and common patterns.

What gets adjusted are the model's internal numbers, called **parameters**. A large model has billions of them, and this is the one fact about training that affects your work: every parameter must sit in memory (@fig-model-memory).

![Memory needed for a model with 8 billion parameters. Running it fits on one large GPU. Training it does not.](/figures/m02/model-memory.pdf){#fig-model-memory}

Each parameter usually takes 2 bytes, so a model with 8 billion of them needs about 16 GB to run. Compressed to half a byte each, it needs about 4 GB. Training needs about 16 bytes per parameter, roughly 128 GB, more than one large GPU holds [@rajbhandari2020]. That is why most companies run models that someone else trained.

## How a word gets its meaning from its neighbours

"Bank" means the side of a river in "the river bank", and a place for money in "my bank account". The model works out which meaning applies the same way you do: by looking at the words around it. In @fig-attention, "bank" pays most of its attention to "river".

![Each word looks at the other words to understand itself. Here "bank" looks mostly at "river". (Numbers made up for illustration.)](/figures/m02/attention.pdf){#fig-attention}

This idea is called **attention**. It is the heart of the **transformer**, the design almost every modern model uses.

Attention has a cost you will meet in practice. To write each new word, the model looks back at every word before it. To save time, it keeps notes on the earlier words in memory, and the notes grow with every word. For a typical 8-billion-parameter model:

1. One conversation of 8,000 tokens needs about 1 GB of notes.
2. Fifty such conversations at once need about 50 GB, three times the memory of the model itself.

That is why long conversations are expensive, and why every model limits how much text it accepts.

*Try it:* Transformer Explainer (poloclub.github.io/transformer-explainer) runs a small model in your browser. Type a sentence and watch the attention lines move between words, then see the chances for the next token [@cho2025].

## Meaning as a map

"I want my money back" and "refund chahiye" share no words, yet mean the same thing. A search for matching words would never link them.

An **embedding** turns a piece of text into a long list of numbers, so that texts with similar meaning get similar lists. Think of each list as a point on a map. In @fig-embedding-map, refund messages land in one area, delivery complaints in another, and product questions in a third, whatever language they are written in.

![Messages placed by meaning. Real embeddings have hundreds of numbers; this picture squeezes them into two so they can be drawn. (Positions illustrative.)](/figures/m02/embedding-map.pdf){#fig-embedding-map}

To check whether two messages mean the same thing, you measure how close their points are. The usual measure is **cosine similarity**, which gives a score near 1 for very similar meanings.

How long should the list of numbers be? Longer lists capture finer differences in meaning, but take more space and more time to search. A million stored pieces of text take about 6 GB with 1,536 numbers each, and about 1.5 GB with 384. Pick the smallest size that still finds the right results on your own data.

Embeddings come from separate, smaller models that only produce these lists. Module 6 builds search on top of them.

*Try it:* the Embedding Projector (projector.tensorflow.org) shows thousands of words as points in 3D. Search for a word and see which words sit closest to it.

## More text can mean worse answers

Every model has a **context window**: the most tokens it can take in one call. Some now hold a million tokens or more. So it is tempting to send everything: all the policies, all the past emails, every order.

Look at @fig-context-share. When a 30-token question sits beside 300 tokens of material, it is 9% of what the model reads. Beside 300,000 tokens, it is 0.01%. The question is still there, but it is a tiny part of what the model's attention is spread over.

![How much of the input is the actual question, with a little material and with a lot.](/figures/m02/context-share.pdf){#fig-context-share}

Experiments show the result. As the input grows, answers get worse, even on simple tasks, and even far below the window's limit [@chroma2025]. This is called **context rot**.

So a big window does not mean you can stop choosing what to send. Module 3 is about choosing well.

## Reading is fast, writing is slow

@fig-prefill-decode shows the difference between how a model handles your input and its own output.

![The model reads all the input in one go, but writes the output one token at a time.](/figures/m02/prefill-decode.pdf){#fig-prefill-decode}

Your input is known from the start, so the model reads all of it in one go. Its output is not. It must write token 1 before it can write token 2, so it works through the output one token at a time. Each output token takes much more computer time than each input token. That is why providers charge around four to five times more for output.

You will notice two speeds:

- **Time to first token**: how long before anything appears. It grows with the length of your input, because all of it is read first.
- **Tokens per second**: how fast the rest arrives once it starts.

Showing the reply word by word as it is written, called **streaming**, makes a slow reply feel fast, because the user starts reading early.

Providers also cut costs behind the scenes. They reuse the work when many requests start with the same text (**prefix caching**; Module 3 shows how to benefit), and they compress the model's numbers to save memory and time (**quantisation**, the "compressed" bar in @fig-model-memory).

## Same question, different answer, even at temperature 0

At temperature 0, the model should always pick its top token, so the same question should always get the same answer. Often it does not.

The reason is in how providers run models. Your request is processed together with other people's requests, and the size of that group changes every moment. That changes the order in which the computer adds up its numbers, which can change the result in the last few digits. Usually this changes nothing. But when two tokens are almost tied, the tiny difference can flip the choice, and the rest of the reply goes another way [@he2025].

The lesson is simple: never build anything that needs the model to give exactly the same text twice. Check the meaning of the answer instead. Module 9 shows how.

## Thinking costs tokens

What is 2 + 2? You answer at once. What is 17 × 24? You probably work it out in steps. Models are similar: on problems with several steps, they do better if they write out their working first.

**Thinking models** do this automatically. Before the answer, they write hidden reasoning, and a setting usually called **effort** controls how much. You pay for that reasoning like any other output. @fig-thinking-cost shows what that means for a simple job, sorting a message into one of four categories.

![Output tokens for sorting one message, with and without heavy thinking. The answer is the same one word.](/figures/m02/thinking-cost.pdf){#fig-thinking-cost}

The answer is the same one word, at 76 times the output cost. For sorting messages, that is waste. For working out a refund across three partial returns and a coupon, the thinking may be what makes the answer right. So compare models by the **cost per finished task**, not by the price per token.

## Big models that still run fast

A bigger model usually gives better answers. But every word passes through the whole model, so a bigger model is also slower and costs more per word.

A **mixture of experts** gets around this. The model is split into many parts, called experts, and for each token a small router sends the work to only a few of them (@fig-moe). Mixtral 8x7B, for example, has about 47 billion parameters in total, but uses about 13 billion for each token [@jiang2024].

![A mixture of experts. Each token goes to only two of the eight experts, but all eight must be kept in memory.](/figures/m02/moe.pdf){#fig-moe}

The catch: speed depends on the part that is used, but memory depends on the whole. Every expert must be loaded, because the next token might need a different one. Such a model can be as fast as a small model and still need the memory of a large one.

## Images, documents and speech

The same design handles more than text. An image is cut into small squares, and each square is treated like a token, so the model can answer a question about a photo. A scanned page can be read the same way. Speech is cut into short slices of sound, or turned into text first by a separate model.

Images are not free. One image can cost as many tokens as a full page of text, so a screenshot with every question adds up quickly.

## Choosing a model

There is no single best model. There is only the right model for each job.

- **Sorting, extracting and short answers**: a small, fast, cheap model. A large one gives the same answer at many times the cost.
- **Problems with several steps, or writing that must be exact**: a large model, sometimes with thinking turned on.
- **Open-weight models**, which you can download and run yourself: data stays in-house, and they can be cheaper at high volume. But you run the hardware, and "open" does not always mean free for commercial use. Read the licence.
- **Models through an API**: no hardware to manage. Usually the best place to start.

The only reliable way to choose is to test. Try a few models on your own real examples, and compare quality, speed and cost per finished task. Module 9 shows how.

The model knows only what is in front of it at the moment you call it. So what should you put in front of it, and in what order? That is Module 3.
